content: The left lung is anatomically divided into two distinct lobes: the upper (superior) lobe and the lower (inferior) lobe. From there, it runs backward and upward toward the posterior border of the lung, crossing it approximately 6 cm below the apex. It then continues downward and forward across the costal surface, reaching the lower border slightly behind the anterior extremity. It encompasses the apex of the lung, the anterior border, a significant portion of the costal surface, and the majority of the mediastinal surface. It constitutes nearly the entire base of the lung, a substantial portion of the costal surface, and most of the posterior border. On the mediastinal surface of the left lung, several notable impressions are present due to adjacent anatomical structures. Immediately above the hilum, there is a distinct curved groove created by the aortic arch. Extending upward from this groove toward the apex is another groove that accommodates the left subclavian artery. An additional, smaller impression located anterior to the subclavian artery groove and near the lung's margin houses the left innominate vein. Posterior to the hilum and the pulmonary ligament, a vertical groove is formed by the descending aorta. Anterior to this groove, near the base of the lung, the lower portion of the esophagus creates a shallow impression on the lung's surface.
